content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a method to learn soft prompts for CLIP using a few labeled images from a downstream image classification dataset.
Different from existing prompt-learning method for CLIP, the proposed method uses hand-crafted prompts during training, by matching the features of soft prompts with those of the hand-crafted ones. The proposed method shows some improvement on few-shot image classification, especially on the accuracy for novel classes from the same dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- It is a good idea to make use of hand-crafted prompts during soft prompt learning. Human knowledge could be important especially when training data is scarce.
- It is important that the paper focuses on the classification performance on the novel classes. 
- The paper is mostly well-written.

Weaknesses:

- The term "language-aware soft prompting" is misleading. Different from previous work (e.g., CoOp), the proposed method uses "hand-crafted" prompts during training. Therefore, the proposed method is a form of *knowledge distillation* from human-created prompts to soft prompts. 

- The problem should instead be formulated as: how to make use of hand-crafted prompts (i.e., human knowledge) during soft prompt tuning. This paper proposes to align the text embedding of the soft prompt with the text embeddings of human prompts. There exist other possible methods, such as appending the human prompts to the soft prompt. 

- If the authors perform LASP+ but without fine-tuning on images (i.e., only learn a soft prompt using the text encoder to match hand-crafted prompts). Could the learned soft prompt reaches similar or better *zero-shot* performance compared to hand-crafted prompts? It would make the paper much stronger if the proposed method can achieve zero-shot prompt learning.

- The improvement of LASP seems marginal. While LASP+ does achieve better performance on novel classes, it is not a fair comparison as LASP+ has access to novel class information during training.

- I'm a bit confused on the difference in evaluation settings between Table 1 and 2. Could the authors elaborate?

- I assume that this would be quite challenging, but any chance that the prompt learned on one dataset can be transferred to other datasets?
 
- The title is too broad. "Vision&Language Foundation Models" cover a much wider range of models than CLIP. It is suggested to change the title to be more specifically related to contrastive VL models for few-shot image classification.

- Some claims are ambiguous and lack support, such as "we propose to exploit the intrinsic model of the world".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed method is not very novel. The method is clearly described with some inaccurate claims.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper addresses an important problem of few-shot adaptation for a CLIP model. The proposed method has some merit in making use of human-designed prompts during training. However, the paper is not well-positioned as a study to exploit human prompt. The empirical performance is not strong enough, and the comparison with existing methods might be unfair. Therefore I'm leaning towards rejection.

content.title: Reply to R3 (CNng) - part 1
content.comment:
We thank for reviewing for acknowledging that our idea is good and that the paper is well written. We hope that we addressed your remaining concerns bellow.

**R3.1.** The term "language-aware soft prompting" is misleading. Different from previous work (e.g., CoOp), the proposed method uses "hand-crafted" prompts during training. Therefore, the proposed method is a form of knowledge distillation from human-created prompts to soft prompts.

**A3.1.** We would like to point here that this is not a distillation target in the classical sense, as there is no image-text soft label or feature. Instead, we are directly asking the model to identify the correct class given a set of templates. At most this is akin to a data-free distillation (data-free with respect to the images), where we operate solely on the classifier weights, produced by the text encoder. The templates can be hand crafted or completely random (the latter is tested in Table 5). This is analogous to the vision-text loss but performed solely in the text space. We offer an interpretation of the loss in Section 3.2 (as a regularizer, as a language-based augmentation and as a way of learning discriminative class centroids).

**R.3.2.** The problem should instead be formulated as: how to make use of hand-crafted prompts (i.e., human knowledge) during soft prompt tuning. This paper proposes to align the text embedding of the soft prompt with the text embeddings of human prompts. There exist other possible methods, such as appending the human prompts to the soft prompt.

**A3.2.** We agree with you but we also make this connection. From intro: “since prompt learning improves the accuracy on base classes but prompt engineering is better on novel classes, we propose to learn the soft prompts by adding a cross entropy text-to-text loss that enforces the learned prompts to be close, in embedding space, to the hand-engineered ones, thus exploiting the intrinsic information captured by the text encoder”

**R.3.3.** If the authors perform LASP+ but without fine-tuning on images (i.e., only learn a soft prompt using the text encoder to match hand-crafted prompts). Could the learned soft prompt reaches similar or better zero-shot performance compared to hand-crafted prompts? It would make the paper much stronger if the proposed method can achieve zero-shot prompt learning.

**A.3.3.** That’s a very good point. The answer is Yes!

Generally, we expect this to be somewhat dependent on how the templates are generated. As one can perform augmentation in the text domain analogous to the image domain. E.g.: We can augment the concept of a dog but changing its color or style or pose in the text domain: “a red dog”, “a dog sitting straight”,  or even increasing their count: “two dogs”. We have a full discussion regarding this concept of augmentation in Section 3.2, page 5 (LASP as language-based augmentation).

Without performing any explicit selection, directly using the set of sentences we measured gains on multiple datasets DTD (from 59.9 for CLIP to 62.0 Ours), EuroSAT (64.05% for CLIP to 71.0% Ours), UCF101 (77.50 for CLIP to 78.0) etc. We measure small gains for all datasets, except for StanfordCars (5% drop) and FGVC Aircraft (5.2% drop). The latter are due to the class names used in the two datasets (model number) which are harder to interpret semantically without context, using generic sentences. We hope you find these results interesting. Thank you for your suggestion, we will add them to the updated paper.
 
**R3.4.** The improvement of LASP seems marginal. While LASP+ does achieve better performance on novel classes, it is not a fair comparison as LASP+ has access to novel class information during training.

**A3.4.** A look at our results reveals that the accuracy improvements are quite large: 1. LASP significantly improves upon our direct baseline, CoOp, by +4.5% on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed text-to-text loss. 2. LASP+, trained with virtual classes, outperforms CoOp by 6.5%, and the more computationally demanding CoCoOp by 1.5%. It also outperforms CLIP for the case of novel classes in 8 out of 11 datasets. 3. It is orders of magnitude faster than CoCoOp (for large numbers of classes, >100; see Fig. 4) 
Note that CoOp is considered the direct baseline as it has the same complexity as our method. CoCoOp needs image-based condition for the text-encoder which makes it very slow. 

Moreover,  the comparison between LASP+ and the rest of the methods is fair. Knowing the class name is a requirement for performing zero-shot classification, and one could treat is a form of zero-shot adaptation, as we don't require any images for that classes. Plus, as we show in Table 3 and 4, we can increase the number of virtual classes outside of the original set without losing performance on it - which is a unique feature and advantage of our approach.

content.title: About using novel class names during training
content.comment:
Thanks the authors for the prompt response!

Let me further clarify my concern on the fairness of comparison. LASP+ uses novel class names during *training* to learn the prompts. This is different from using novel class names during *inference*. One may argue that the class names are no longer "novel" if they are exposed during training. None of the baselines seem to have this assumption.

Furthermore, the baseline methods (CoOp and CoCoOp) do not seem to use hand-crafted prompt (please correct me if I'm wrong). Given the additional human knowledge, I believe that reported performance improvement from LASP is expected and thus not significant.

If the authors could provide an updated manuscript (I know this is a huge ask) to provide a more comprehensive study regarding my comments "R.3.2" and "R.3.3". I would consider raising my score. Otherwise I tend to remain my current score.

content.title: Additional clarifications
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to check our rebuttal.

We would like to make the following clarifications:

- Training with virtual classes does not violate the zero-shot setting, according to [1]: ``Zero-shot learning aims to recognize objects whose **instances** may not have been seen during training''. We do not use any images for the novel classes. Moreover, from a practical perspective, if the novel class names are not known during initial training, the model can be simply retrained in a zero-shot manner when they become available.  
None of the baselines have this assumption as this is actually our idea :) We are the first to propose both the concept and a mechanism to realize it in practice. 

- There is no human knowledge in this sense. The textual prompts are the original ones used by CLIP, they are not tweaked nor changed: neither globally, nor on a dataset by dataset basis. Moreover, as we show in Table 5, even when using completely random sentences, our approach can still show consistent gains (see appendix for example of such random sentences).


- Firstly, if something is intuitive, it does not diminish its value. Secondly, a simple fusion of hand-engineered and learned prompts does not work well. Thirdly, an L1 loss between hand-engineered and learned prompts works poorly (see A1.2). Fourthly, if it is obvious then we would expect other works to have proposed it or report it as baseline (prior works + other existing ICLR submissions). 

[1] Zero-Shot Learning -- The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, Yongqin Xian, Bernt Schiele, Zeynep Akata, CVPR 2017

content.title: Reply to R3 (CNng) - part 2
content.comment:
**R.3.5.** I'm a bit confused on the difference in evaluation settings between Table 1 and 2. Could the authors elaborate?

**A.3.5.** In Table 1 the model is restricted to select a class from its own set of classes. For example, when evaluating on the base classes, the model will consider only the base class names, not the base and novel. When testing on the images from the novel classes, we only consider the novel class names. This is the standard protocol used in prior work.

As we think this doesn’t full capture potential bias toward the base classes, in Table 2 no matter the set of images we evaluate on, either base or novel, the model always has to select from the combined set of novel+base classes. In literature this is often called generalized zero shot recognition.
 
**R.3.6.** I assume that this would be quite challenging, but any chance that the prompt learned on one dataset can be transferred to other datasets?

**A3.6.** Thank you for your question. We do test for this in fact. See the results from Table 6 and 7, where the prompts learned on imagenet are tested on different datasets. Our model nearly always outperforms its direct competitor, CoOp, while matching and outperforming CoCop too for more than half of the datasets, while being significantly faster than the later.

**R.3.7.** The title is too broad. "Vision&Language Foundation Models" cover a much wider range of models than CLIP. It is suggested to change the title to be more specifically related to contrastive VL models for few-shot image classification.

**A3.7.** Thank you for your suggestion, we will adjust the title to reflect the fact that we focus on the constrastive family of VL models.

**R.3.8.** Some claims are ambiguous and lack support, such as "we propose to exploit the intrinsic model of the world".

**A.3.8.** We meant that the language model learns relations between different objects and concepts from the input sentences it was trained one. We agree however that this particular wording is somewhat ambiguous/inexact. We will address this in the updated manuscript.

**R.3.9.** The proposed method is not very novel. The method is clearly described with some inaccurate claims.

**A3.9.** We respectfully disagree. Because our method is simple it doesn’t mean it’s not novel. We believe that our paper’s highlight LASP+ which trains on virtual classes significantly stands out from previous work on prompting for V&L models.

**R3.10.** The empirical performance is not strong enough, and the comparison with existing methods might be unfair. Therefore I'm leaning towards rejection.

**A3.10.** A look at our results reveals that the accuracy improvements are quite large: 1. LASP significantly improves upon our direct baseline, CoOp, by +4.5% on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed text-to-text loss. 2. LASP+, trained with virtual classes, outperforms CoOp by 6.5%, and the more computationally demanding CoCoOp by 1.5%. It also outperforms CLIP for the case of novel classes in 8 out of 11 datasets. 3. It is orders of magnitude faster than CoCoOp (for large numbers of classes, >100; see Fig. 4) 
Note that CoOp is considered the direct baseline as it has the same complexity as our method. CoCoOp needs image-based condition for the text-encoder which makes it very slow.

Our comparisons are fair. We respect the protocol described in CoOp and CoCoOp, using the same splits, the same augmentation and event schedulers. We even go beyond and analyze the performance of the method under new settings: generalized zero-shot evaluation (Table 2) and with distractors (i.e. additional class names that are not present in the images are used, which is a more realistic setting for zero shot evaluation – see Table 3 and 4). Please lso see A3..

We appreciate your feedback and questions and hope our answer addresses your concerns, hoping that you will upgrade your score in the light of this.

We remain available and are happy to offer additional clarifications if needed.

content.title: Reply to R1 (rKqH) - part 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing that the proposed idea is intuitive and straightforward, verified by extensive empirical results. We hope to have addressed your remaining concerns below.

**R.1.** Does the distillation target have to be from the same pretrained encoder? What if using other pretrained text encoder to produce the target embedding with additional projection layers?

**A.1.** Yes, the target must be from the same pretrained encoder. The reason for this is the following: CLIP learns a joint embedding space in which similar visual and language samples lie close together. Optimizing against samples that are outside this space will make the text encoder features deviate from this, making them incompatible with the visual encoder features and reducing its efficacy.

Similarly, using a linear layer to map them to the same space leads to severe overfitting (generally the main challenge with all these adaptations methods is avoiding overfitting). This highlights the importance of applying the loss in the proposed way.

We would also like to point here that this is not a distillation target in the classical sense, as there is no image-text soft label or feature. Instead, we are directly asking the model to identify the correct class given a set of templates. At most this is akin to a data-free distillation (data-free with respect to the images), where we operate solely on the classifier weights, produced by the text encoder. The templates can be hand crafted or completely random (the latter is tested in Table 5). This is analogous to the vision-text loss but performed solely in the text space. We offer an interpretation of the loss in Section 3.2 (as a regularizer, as a language-based augmentation and as a way of learning discriminative class centroids).


**R1.2.** What if simply ensemble the results from soft prompts and the results from hand-crafted prompts?

**A1.2.** We have tried this, but this results in significant performance degradation for the base classes.  This isn’t too surprising, as the results from Table 1 indicate, the performance of CLIP (i.e., hard prompts) on the base classes is 69.34 only, while of ours 81.42. Averaging the predictions of these two models drops the accuracy by more than 5% (!). This shows that out approach is required to obtain high accuracy on the base classes, while preserving the generalizability on the novel ones.

**A1.3.** Does virtual classes have to be from class names? What if we further scale up the size of virtual classes?.

**R1.3.** No, any class names can be used, and the list can be expanded easily. We have already tested this in Table 4 (where we use additional class names within domain) and Table 3 (with out-domain class names). There we show our method can successfully scale to significant increases in the number of classes (tested up to 20x for EuroSAT).

**R.1.4.** What is the upper bound of such soft prompt? For example, directly learn a soft prompt on the joint set of base and new classes.

**A.1.4.** We have already tested this. LASP+ is our method trained on the image belonging to the base classes + the class names of both the base and novel classes. In contrast, LASP, was trained on the images belonging to the base classes and only the class names of the base set.
Training using the images across both base and novel performs similarly with CoOp, as our approach is particularly targeted at improving the performance on novel classes, while retaining that on the base classes.

**R.1.5.** How does this regularization compare to other regularization? For example, learning soft-prompt in a residual manner from a hand crafted prompt with L1/L2 regularization.

**A.1.5.** Our loss does behave in part as a regularize too (see Section 3.2). In contrast with a L_p distance, that only brings together pairs of samples (prediction, gt) minimizing their L_p distance,  our loss forces the model to make samples belonging to the correct class close together, while pushing the rest apart. As at each step the model needs to learn to select the sentence containing the correct class.

In a sense, the general reason is the same as for why we are using a cross entropy loss to learn a classifier instead of an L_p distance.

When tested with a L_p loss, the performance on the novel classes degrades by approx. 4%. We thank you for your suggestion, we will add this result in the paper, alongside with a discussion motivating our choice.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2918 by Reviewer rKqH

content.title: Reply to R1 (rKqH) - part 2
content.comment:
**R.1.6.** Overall, the technical novelty is limited as the proposed method is essentially knowledge distillation without justification of the choice of loss formulation. Does it really have to be a single-class classification formulation?

**A1.6.** We politely disagree.  Our approach is not simply a form of distillation, but a principled way of performing a text-to-text optimization analogous to the vision-text loss, that leverages the joint vision-language space  learned by CLIP in which bringing a sample closer in the text-space also brings it closer in the vision one generally. The intuition of our loss is described in Section 3.2.

We would also like to point out that our work is the first to investigate such an idea, of text-to-text optimisation in the context of adapting the VL model for image based tasks.

We hope that the above replies, alongside the new results with the L_p loss addressed your concerns and that we convinced you to upgrade your score accordingly. We will include the results, the discussion and the clarifications in the paper. We are more than happy to clarify any remaining or follow up question.
